# arbitrary - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arbitrary/

## Expand description

The `Arbitrary` trait crate.

This trait provides an [ Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html) trait to
produce well-typed, structured values, from raw, byte buffers. It is
generally intended to be used with fuzzers like AFL or libFuzzer. See the

[trait’s documentation for details on automatically deriving, implementing, and/or using the trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`Arbitrary`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [size_](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html)- hint
- Utilities for working with and combining the results of
`Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [unstructured](https://docs.rs/unstructured/index.html)
- Wrappers around raw, unstructured bytes.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [MaxRecursion](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)- Reached
- Error indicating that the maximum recursion depth has been reached while calculating `Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)
- A source of unstructured data.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- An enumeration of buffer creation errors

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A `Result`with the error type fixed as`arbitrary::Error`.

# arbitrary 1.4.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arbitrary/latest

## About

The `Arbitrary` crate lets you construct arbitrary instances of a type.

This crate is primarily intended to be combined with a fuzzer like [libFuzzer
and  cargo-fuzz](https://github.com/rust-fuzz/cargo-fuzz) or

[AFL](https://github.com/rust-fuzz/afl.rs), and to help you turn the raw, untyped byte buffers that they produce into well-typed, valid, structured values. This allows you to combine structure-aware test case generation with coverage-guided, mutation-based fuzzers.

## Documentation

## Example

Say you're writing a color conversion library, and you have an `Rgb` struct to
represent RGB colors. You might want to implement `Arbitrary` for `Rgb` so that
you could take arbitrary `Rgb` instances in a test function that asserts some
property (for example, asserting that RGB converted to HSL and converted back to
RGB always ends up exactly where we started).

### Automatically Deriving `Arbitrary`

Automatically deriving the `Arbitrary` trait is the recommended way to implement
`Arbitrary` for your types.

Automatically deriving `Arbitrary` requires you to enable the `"derive"` cargo
feature:

```
# Cargo.toml
[]
 = {  = "1",  = ["derive"] }
```
And then you can simply add `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` annotations to your types:

```
// rgb.rs
use Arbitrary;
```
#### Customizing single fields

This can be particular handy if your structure uses a type that does not implement `Arbitrary` or you want to have more customization for particular fields.

```
```
### Implementing `Arbitrary` By Hand

Alternatively, you can write an `Arbitrary` implementation by hand:

```
// rgb.rs
use ;
```
## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate is guaranteed to compile on stable Rust **1.63.0** and up. It might
compile with older versions but that may change in any new patch release.

We reserve the right to increment the MSRV on minor releases, however we will strive to only do it deliberately and for good reasons.

## License

Licensed under dual MIT or Apache-2.0 at your choice.

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in this project by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# kglite - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kglite/0.12.10/kglite/

## Expand description

kglite — pure-Rust knowledge graph engine.

Cypher pipeline, snapshot/working CoW transactions, columnar /
mmap / disk storage backends, optional dataset loaders
(SEC EDGAR, Sodir, Wikidata). The Python wheel
(`pip install kglite`) is built by the sibling `kglite-py`
crate; the Bolt and MCP protocol servers are separate
workspace binaries.

[§](https://docs.rs#public-api)Public API

Downstream Rust consumers (the Python wheel, the bolt and
mcp server binaries, future Go/TypeScript/JVM bindings)
should depend on the curated [ api](https://docs.rs/api/index.html) module — those items
get semver guarantees. Anything else is an implementation
detail.

See `docs/rust/embedding.md` for the embedder guide.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [api](https://docs.rs/api/index.html)
- Curated stable Rust API. Downstream consumers should depend on items here, not on the underlying module structure (which may move between minor releases).
- [code_](https://docs.rs/code_tree/index.html)- tree
- Code-tree: parse polyglot codebases into KGLite knowledge graphs.
- [datatypes](https://docs.rs/datatypes/index.html)
- Datatypes shared across the kglite engine.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Typed error taxonomy for KGLite.
- [graphgen](https://docs.rs/graphgen/index.html)
- Streaming synthetic property-graph generator — bundled so any binding can
produce a realistic benchmark / demo graph in one call (mirrors how
`code_tree`lives in the core crate and is surfaced through the wheel).
- [okf](https://docs.rs/okf/index.html)
- OKF (Open Knowledge Format) bundle ingestion — read-only, partial.
- [param](https://docs.rs/param/index.html)
- Parameter-shape helpers for bindings — wire-shaped values
(JSON / protobuf-map / etc.) → `kglite::api::Value`.

# looop 0.43.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/looop/0.43.1

# looop

A tiny, portable, autonomous control loop for agent-driven work. One self-contained binary — no database, no server, no helper files.

## The idea

**looop is the brain, not a task runner.** It watches the things you care about
(GitHub, Linear, Grafana, …) and runs a fleet of worker agents. Each beat it
senses the world and, if something changed, decides the *single* most important
move and executes it — including spawning workers. The judgment lives *inside*
looop (a small, gated LLM call per beat).

An autonomous loop is easy. The hard part — and the whole point of looop's
design — is **where and how a human enters the loop.** Too much human and it
isn't autonomous; too little and it's reckless. looop's answer is to pull you in
at exactly two kinds of moments, and nowhere else.

## How the human stays in the loop

There are two distinct ways you touch the loop — and that split *is* the design.

**Steer — async, you initiate.** You are a peer, not a driver. You shape *what*
looop pursues by editing goals and the PLAYBOOK; it observes them next beat. This
never blocks the loop — you set direction and walk away.

**Answer — sync, the loop initiates.** looop reaches back for *you* only when it
genuinely must: a worker hits a decision only a human can make, or an
irreversible action — merge, deploy, delete — needs an explicit yes. It blocks
and waits for your call.

The key move: **the intervention point is decoupled from any UI.** Asks and
answers are a durable file mailbox reached through one backend-agnostic contract
(`looop _ …`), so the loop never blocks on a particular terminal, tmux, or stdin
— it just needs an answer *eventually*, from whatever channel reaches you:

- a **bare terminal**— you typing the verbs yourself (the thinnest client);
- an **agent concierge**— a`claude`/`codex`/`opencode`/`pi`session that relays asks in plain language and answers on your behalf;
- a **notify script**— a loop that pushes asks to Slack/SMS and relays your reply.

A client is an *interface*, never a decision-maker. looop decides; the client
just carries the question to you and your answer back.

Two properties make all this dependable:

- **Level-triggered.**All state is plain files, so the loop re-senses every beat and a crashed pulse just re-reads its files on restart. A pending ask survives restarts — no queues, no lost work.
- **One move per beat.**Each beat does at most one thing; a daily budget caps spend. Behavior stays legible and cheap — an unchanged world costs no LLM call.

## One beat: sense → decide → act

- **SENSE**— run every- `sensors/*.sh`, refreshing- `snapshots/`. World unchanged since last beat → stop here, no LLM call.
- **DECIDE**— on change, hand the PLAYBOOK + goals + readings + pending asks to the LLM, which returns- **one**typed move.
- **ACT**— execute it: write a goal/sensor/PLAYBOOK, run one reversible command, or spawn a worker. Irreversible moves are gated — they wait for your- `answer`(see above), and so does any worker that hits a human-only decision.

## Three layers

| Layer | What it is |
|---|---|
| core | the autonomous pulse + the durable state behind it. Decides and acts. |
| contract | the `looop _ …`verbs — the one stable, backend-agnostic surface to read and steer core. |
| client | anything that drives the contract for a human (terminal / concierge / notify). An interface, never a decision-maker. |

State is plain files in the data dir, reached *through* the contract — not a
public interface:

| File / dir | Role |
|---|---|
| `PLAYBOOK.md` | your judgment, priorities, guardrails |
| `goals/*.md` | desired state — one declarative spec per thing you push |
| `sensors/*.sh` | observers — each prints one JSON object |
| `journal.md` | action log — one line per move |
| `asks/``answers/` | the worker ↔ human mailbox |

## Install

```
 |
# or
```
**Only hard dependency:** an LLM runner. `claude` is the default; `codex`,
`opencode`, and `pi` also work — pick one with `looop init`. (Workers that touch
code isolate their own sandbox via `git worktree` — a worker convention, not a
looop dependency.)

## Usage

The pulse refuses to start until `looop init` writes the runner wiring, so the
agent CLI driving every tick and worker is always an explicit choice. Read and
steer core with the `looop _ …` verbs (`_ state`, `_ wait`, `_ answer`,
`_ goal write`), by hand or through a client.

### First run

looop runs headless, so it can't interview you. A fresh data dir is seeded with a
starter PLAYBOOK, a `setup` goal, and a real pending `setup` ask so a client
waiting on asks wakes immediately.

Start with `looop up` then `looop client`: the TUI keeps the pending ask list on
screen and lets you answer by hand — no extra tooling, just looop. Answer the
starter `setup` ask, edit your goals/PLAYBOOK with the `looop _ …` verbs, archive
the `setup` goal, and looop runs from there.

**Even easier: an agent concierge.** Point a `claude`/`codex`/`opencode`/`pi`
session at looop and talk to it in plain language — it relays asks with
recommendations, drives the write verbs for you, and interviews you to shape your
goals, sensors, and PLAYBOOK:

```
# "be my looop concierge: run `looop up`, relay the setup goal, and interview
#  me to write my goals, sensors, and PLAYBOOK."
```
See `looop help` for the full command reference and design manual.

## Configuration

The config (`$LOOOP_CONFIG`, default `~/.config/looop/config.json`) is just **two
shell commands**. `looop init` lets you pick `claude`, `codex`, `opencode`, `pi`,
or `custom`; after that looop treats the result as plain runner wiring:

| Key | Role |
|---|---|
| `tick_command` | run ONE disposable decision. The prompt is passed via the `{{prompt_file}}`placeholder (substituted with the prompt file path — read it with`$(cat {{prompt_file}})`or`@{{prompt_file}}`). If you omit the placeholder the prompt is piped in onstdininstead. Must run unattended (no permission prompts — the detached pulse can't answer them) and emit a structured event stream looop can render. |
| `worker_command` | launch a worker agent. Same `{{prompt_file}}`placeholder, substituted with the worker's prompt file path. (A worker can't use the stdin fallback — stdin is its live attach TTY.) It may also carry`{{model}}`and`{{thinking}}`placeholders for per-worker model selection (see below). |

**Per-worker model selection.** The `worker_command` may include `{{model}}` and `{{thinking}}` placeholders. When a worker starts they are substituted with, in precedence order: the `looop _ worker start --model M --thinking L` flags, then the optional top-level `worker_model` / `worker_thinking` config keys, then the empty string. A template that omits a placeholder is left untouched, so configs and flag-less starts behave exactly as before; passing `--model` against a template with no `{{model}}` placeholder logs a warning and is ignored. Example wiring:

```
```
The built-in presets are:

**claude** (default)

```
```
**codex**

```
```
**opencode** (best-effort — verify against your installed version)

```
```
**pi**

```
```
Model ids above are examples. For claude, `sonnet`/`opus` are aliases that always
resolve to the latest of each; pin a specific version (e.g.
`--model claude-opus-4-1`) if you need reproducibility.

# sail - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sail-rs/0.2.10/sail/

## Expand description

`sail-core`: the canonical, typed Sail SDK.

[ Client](https://docs.rs/client/struct.Client.html) is the entry point: a cheap-to-clone async handle that owns
configuration and transport (HTTP for lifecycle/app, gRPC for the
per-sailbox worker proxy). Bindings (the Python extension, the CLI) are thin
layers over it.

As a library, `sail-core` documents its whole public API and never writes to
the process streams or exits: callers decide how to surface output and
errors.

The transport plumbing the bindings reach into lives under the hidden
[`internal`] module; it is not part of the public API and carries no
stability guarantee.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use client::`- [Client](https://docs.rs/client/struct.Client.html);
- `pub use client::`- [ClientBuilder](https://docs.rs/client/struct.ClientBuilder.html);
- `pub use`- [time](https://docs.rs/time/0.3.51/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/time/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [app](https://docs.rs/app/index.html)
- Typed app discovery over the central API.
- [client](https://docs.rs/client/index.html)
- The Sail client: the canonical async surface that owns configuration and transport, shared by every binding (Python, CLI, future hosts).
- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- SDK configuration loaded from environment variables.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Canonical, language-neutral error taxonomy for the Sail core.
- [exec](https://docs.rs/exec/index.html)
- Streaming exec engine: a running command in a sailbox with live output.
- [image](https://docs.rs/image/index.html)
- Typed image specification for
`CreateSailboxRequest`
- [sailbox](https://docs.rs/sailbox/index.html)
- Typed sailbox surface: domain models and the HTTP API client.
- [worker](https://docs.rs/worker/index.html)
- Per-sailbox worker-proxy client: the gRPC operations that terminate at a sailbox’s own worker proxy (exec wait/cancel, listeners, files), sharing one lazily-dialed, drain-aware channel cache and the API-key credential.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [block_](https://docs.rs/fn.block_on.html)- on
- Drive a future to completion on the shared runtime, the sync facade for callers outside any async context (the PyO3 bridge with the GIL released, and the CLI).

# kigumi_mod_base - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi-mod-base/1.0.0/kigumi_mod_base/

## Expand description

Base module: the foundational models other modules build on — currency, partner (contacts), and company. Root of the dependency graph (no dependencies of its own).

Multi-company: `res.company` is the unit of data isolation; transactional models carry a
`company_id` (added per model, e.g. sale.order). Partners are shared (no company_id) to avoid a
circular FK with res.company; company-specific contacts can be modelled later behind a deferred
FK. The active-company filtering rule lives in the security layer (Ctx.company + a record rule).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [seed](https://docs.rs/seed/index.html)
- Base reference data, run by the `register_seed!`seam at every migrate while`base`is installed: one default currency + company (multi-company needs a company to exist), a starter country set, and the read-only`res.groups`projection of every registered ACL/rule group. Every block is guarded by an exists-check — the DB is the authority, an operator change is never overwritten. Relocated verbatim from kigumi-cli so adopter binaries get it too.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [IrAttachment](https://docs.rs/struct.IrAttachment.html)
- [ResCompany](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCompany.html)
- [ResCountry](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCountry.html)
- [ResCountry](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCountryState.html)- State
- [ResCurrency](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCurrency.html)
- [ResCurrency](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCurrencyRate.html)- Rate
- [ResGroups](https://docs.rs/struct.ResGroups.html)
- [ResPartner](https://docs.rs/struct.ResPartner.html)
- [ResUsers](https://docs.rs/struct.ResUsers.html)

## Statics[§](https://docs.rs#statics)

- [ACLS](https://docs.rs/static.ACLS.html)
- Base ACLs: the everyday `user`group reads the foundational reference data and the group list; the user directory (`res.users`) is admin-only (read-only — account changes go through auth).`ir.attachment`generic CRUD is admin-only: end users reach files through the gated`/attachments`endpoints (which check host access and run elevated), never the raw model.
- [MANIFEST](https://docs.rs/static.MANIFEST.html)
- Module manifest. `base`depends on nothing and anchors the catalog.

# capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/capnp_rpc/

## Expand description

An implementation of the [Cap’n Proto remote procedure call](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html)
protocol. Includes all [Level 1](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features) features.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
# Cap'n Proto schema
interface Foo {
    identity @0 (x: UInt32) -> (y: UInt32);
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Rust server defining an implementation of Foo.
struct FooImpl;
impl foo::Server for FooImpl {
    async fn identity(
        self: Rc<Self>,
        params: foo::IdentityParams,
        mut results: foo::IdentityResults
    ) -> Result<(), ::capnp::Error> {
        let x = params.get()?.get_x();
        results.get().set_y(x);
        Ok(())
    }
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Rust client calling a remote implementation of Foo.
let mut request = foo_client.identity_request();
request.get().set_x(123);
let promise = request.send().promise.and_then(|response| {
    println!("results = {}", response.get()?.get_y());
    Ok(())
});
```
For a more complete example, see [https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [rpc_](https://docs.rs/rpc_capnp/index.html)- capnp
- Code generated from
[rpc.capnp](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/rpc.capnp).
- [rpc_](https://docs.rs/rpc_twoparty_capnp/index.html)- twoparty_ - capnp
- Code generated from
[rpc-twoparty.capnp](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/rpc-twoparty.capnp).
- [twoparty](https://docs.rs/twoparty/index.html)
- An implementation of `VatNetwork`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [pry](https://docs.rs/macro.pry.html)
- Like `try!()``Promise<T, E>``Result<T, E>`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Capability](https://docs.rs/struct.CapabilityServerSet.html)- Server - Set
- Collection of unwrappable capabilities.
- [Disconnector](https://docs.rs/struct.Disconnector.html)
- A `Future`that can be run to disconnect an`RpcSystem`’s ConnectionState and wait for it to be closed.

- A portal to objects available on the network.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Connection](https://docs.rs/trait.Connection.html)
- A two-way RPC connection.

- Tracks a particular RPC stream in order to implement a flow control algorithm.

- A message received from a `VatNetwork`
- [Outgoing](https://docs.rs/trait.OutgoingMessage.html)- Message
- A message to be sent by a `VatNetwork`

- Trait implemented by the reconnecting client to set new connection out-of-band.

- Network facility between vats, it determines how to form connections between vats.

- Creates a new client that reconnects when getting `ErrorKind::Disconnected`
- [lazy_](https://docs.rs/fn.lazy_auto_reconnect.html)- auto_ - reconnect
- Creates a new client that lazily connect and also reconnects when getting `ErrorKind::Disconnected`

- Creates a `Client`from a future that resolves to a`Client`.

# kigumi_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi-server/0.1.0/kigumi_server/

## Expand description

Headless HTTP layer (axum). Serves the integration surface from a model set: the OpenAPI spec, the model list, per-model UI contracts, and — when a database backend is provided — secured data endpoints that enforce the ACL + record-rule engine.

The server is agnostic of any module: a host wires its catalog in with
`kigumi_core::resolve_all_registered()` and its security policy, then calls [ router](https://docs.rs/fn.router.html) or

[. The core stays headless; this crate is optional.](https://docs.rs/fn.router_with_data.html)

`router_with_data`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FsBlob](https://docs.rs/struct.FsBlobStore.html)- Store
- Filesystem blob store: immutable, deduplicated files at `<root>/ab/cd/<hash>`.
- [Genpdf](https://docs.rs/struct.GenpdfRasterizer.html)- Rasterizer
- Renders the report engine’s structured HTML to a PDF with genpdf.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Rasterizer](https://docs.rs/trait.Rasterizer.html)
- Rasterizes a rendered HTML report into PDF bytes. The seam for PDF output: a concrete backend
(e.g. typst- or headless-Chromium-based) plugs in via `router_with_data_rasterized`. When none is configured the report endpoint serves HTML and answers`?format=pdf`with 501.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [access_](https://docs.rs/fn.access_fingerprint.html)- fingerprint
- A cheap content hash of the DB-backed ACL/rule rows (owned data, no leak). The poll loop compares
it across ticks and only reloads the policy when it changes — so out-of-band edits (the `kigumi acl/rule`CLI, direct SQL) go live without paying the load_*_static string leak on every tick.
- [refresh_](https://docs.rs/fn.refresh_access.html)- access
- Recomputes the effective access policy — compiled-in baseline ∪ DB overrides — and swaps it into
the live snapshots, so a runtime ACL/rule change takes effect without a restart. On a DB load error
it KEEPS the prior good snapshot (it does not degrade to baseline-only — that would silently drop a
live restricting rule) and returns `false`, so the caller can retry on the next tick. Returns`true`only when both halves reloaded. NB it leaks the DB rows’ identifier strings (load_*_static), so the poll loop and the mutation endpoints guard it behind`access_fingerprint`
- [refresh_](https://docs.rs/fn.refresh_custom_fields.html)- custom_ - fields
- Reloads the live custom-field map from the registry (after an add, and at startup).
- [refresh_](https://docs.rs/fn.refresh_view_overrides.html)- view_ - overrides
- Reloads the live view-override map from `ir_ui_view`(after a change, and at startup). Owned data, so unlike the access policy this is leak-free and can run on every poll tick unconditionally.
- [router](https://docs.rs/fn.router.html)
- Metadata-only router: OpenAPI spec, model list, UI contracts. No database.
- [router_](https://docs.rs/fn.router_with_data.html)- with_ - data
- Full router: metadata routes plus secured CRUD data endpoints. `auth_secret`is the HS256 secret used to verify the`Authorization: Bearer <token>`of each data request into a`Ctx`. No PDF rasterizer is configured (report`?format=pdf`answers 501); see`router_with_data_rasterized`
- [router_](https://docs.rs/fn.router_with_data_dynamic.html)- with_ - data_ - dynamic
- Like `router_with_data`**live served catalog**:`installed`(a shared, mutable set of installed module names) gates which models are served, so installing/uninstalling a module via the`/api/modules/*`endpoints takes effect without restarting the process (the host passes the FULL linked catalog as`models`and keeps`installed`in sync with the DB). Used by`kigumi serve`.
- [router_](https://docs.rs/fn.router_with_data_dynamic_rasterized.html)- with_ - data_ - dynamic_ - rasterized
- Like `router_with_data_dynamic``?format=pdf`(None → 501).
- [router_](https://docs.rs/fn.router_with_data_rasterized.html)- with_ - data_ - rasterized
- Like `router_with_data``?format=pdf`(None → those requests get 501).

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [AclState](https://docs.rs/type.AclState.html)
- The effective access policy, swappable at runtime. Held as an `Arc`snapshot behind an`RwLock`: a request clones the current snapshot (cheap refcount bump) and reads it without holding the lock across`.await`, while the poll loop and the mutation endpoints replace the snapshot wholesale — so a DB-backed ACL/rule added via the CLI or the`/api/_acl``/api/_rule`endpoints takes effect with no restart, the same “declarative, no recompile” property as runtime custom fields.
- [Rule](https://docs.rs/type.RuleState.html)- State

# arbitrary 1.4.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arbitrary/1.4.2

## About

The `Arbitrary` crate lets you construct arbitrary instances of a type.

This crate is primarily intended to be combined with a fuzzer like [libFuzzer
and  cargo-fuzz](https://github.com/rust-fuzz/cargo-fuzz) or

[AFL](https://github.com/rust-fuzz/afl.rs), and to help you turn the raw, untyped byte buffers that they produce into well-typed, valid, structured values. This allows you to combine structure-aware test case generation with coverage-guided, mutation-based fuzzers.

## Documentation

## Example

Say you're writing a color conversion library, and you have an `Rgb` struct to
represent RGB colors. You might want to implement `Arbitrary` for `Rgb` so that
you could take arbitrary `Rgb` instances in a test function that asserts some
property (for example, asserting that RGB converted to HSL and converted back to
RGB always ends up exactly where we started).

### Automatically Deriving `Arbitrary`

Automatically deriving the `Arbitrary` trait is the recommended way to implement
`Arbitrary` for your types.

Automatically deriving `Arbitrary` requires you to enable the `"derive"` cargo
feature:

```
# Cargo.toml
[]
 = {  = "1",  = ["derive"] }
```
And then you can simply add `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` annotations to your types:

```
// rgb.rs
use Arbitrary;
```
#### Customizing single fields

This can be particular handy if your structure uses a type that does not implement `Arbitrary` or you want to have more customization for particular fields.

```
```
### Implementing `Arbitrary` By Hand

Alternatively, you can write an `Arbitrary` implementation by hand:

```
// rgb.rs
use ;
```
## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate is guaranteed to compile on stable Rust **1.63.0** and up. It might
compile with older versions but that may change in any new patch release.

We reserve the right to increment the MSRV on minor releases, however we will strive to only do it deliberately and for good reasons.

Licensed under dual MIT or Apache-2.0 at your choice.

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in this project by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# arbitrary - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arbitrary/1.4.2/target-redirect/arbitrary/

## Expand description

The `Arbitrary` trait crate.

This trait provides an [ Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html) trait to
produce well-typed, structured values, from raw, byte buffers. It is
generally intended to be used with fuzzers like AFL or libFuzzer. See the

[trait’s documentation for details on automatically deriving, implementing, and/or using the trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`Arbitrary`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [size_](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html)- hint
- Utilities for working with and combining the results of
`Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [unstructured](https://docs.rs/unstructured/index.html)
- Wrappers around raw, unstructured bytes.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [MaxRecursion](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)- Reached
- Error indicating that the maximum recursion depth has been reached while calculating `Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)
- A source of unstructured data.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- An enumeration of buffer creation errors

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A `Result`with the error type fixed as`arbitrary::Error`.

[53](https://docs.rs#53)
[54](https://docs.rs#54)/// Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.
[55](https://docs.rs#55)///
[56](https://docs.rs#56)/// The `Arbitrary` trait allows you to generate valid structured values, like
[57](https://docs.rs#57)/// `HashMap`s, or ASTs, or `MyTomlConfig`, or any other data structure from
[58](https://docs.rs#58)/// raw, unstructured bytes provided by a fuzzer.
[59](https://docs.rs#59)///
[60](https://docs.rs#60)/// # Deriving `Arbitrary`
[61](https://docs.rs#61)///
[62](https://docs.rs#62)/// Automatically deriving the `Arbitrary` trait is the recommended way to
[63](https://docs.rs#63)/// implement `Arbitrary` for your types.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)///
[65](https://docs.rs#65)/// Using the custom derive requires that you enable the `"derive"` cargo
[66](https://docs.rs#66)/// feature in your `Cargo.toml`:
[67](https://docs.rs#67)///
[68](https://docs.rs#68)/// ```toml
[69](https://docs.rs#69)/// [dependencies]
[70](https://docs.rs#70)/// arbitrary = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
[71](https://docs.rs#71)/// ```
[72](https://docs.rs#72)///
[73](https://docs.rs#73)/// Then, you add the `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` annotation to your `struct` or
[74](https://docs.rs#74)/// `enum` type definition:
[75](https://docs.rs#75)///
[76](https://docs.rs#76)/// ```
[77](https://docs.rs#77)/// # #[cfg(feature = "derive")] mod foo {
[78](https://docs.rs#78)/// use arbitrary::Arbitrary;
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// use std::collections::HashSet;
[80](https://docs.rs#80)///
[81](https://docs.rs#81)/// #[derive(Arbitrary)]
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// pub struct AddressBook {
[83](https://docs.rs#83)///     friends: HashSet<Friend>,
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// }
[85](https://docs.rs#85)///
[86](https://docs.rs#86)/// #[derive(Arbitrary, Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// pub enum Friend {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)///     Buddy { name: String },
[89](https://docs.rs#89)///     Pal { age: usize },
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// }
[91](https://docs.rs#91)/// # }
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// ```
[93](https://docs.rs#93)///
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// Every member of the `struct` or `enum` must also implement `Arbitrary`.
[95](https://docs.rs#95)///
[96](https://docs.rs#96)/// It is also possible to change the default bounds added by the derive:
[97](https://docs.rs#97)///
[98](https://docs.rs#98)/// ```
[99](https://docs.rs#99)/// # #[cfg(feature = "derive")] mod foo {
[100](https://docs.rs#100)/// use arbitrary::Arbitrary;
[101](https://docs.rs#101)///
[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// trait Trait {
[103](https://docs.rs#103)///     type Assoc: for<'a> Arbitrary<'a>;
[104](https://docs.rs#104)/// }
[105](https://docs.rs#105)///
[106](https://docs.rs#106)/// #[derive(Arbitrary)]
[107](https://docs.rs#107)/// // The bounds are used verbatim, so any existing trait bounds will need to be repeated.
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// #[arbitrary(bound = "T: Trait")]
[109](https://docs.rs#109)/// struct Point<T: Trait> {
[110](https://docs.rs#110)///     x: T::Assoc,
[111](https://docs.rs#111)/// }
[112](https://docs.rs#112)/// # }
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// ```
[114](https://docs.rs#114)///
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// # Implementing `Arbitrary` By Hand
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// Implementing `Arbitrary` mostly involves nested calls to other `Arbitrary`
[118](https://docs.rs#118)/// arbitrary implementations for each of your `struct` or `enum`'s members. But
[119](https://docs.rs#119)/// sometimes you need some amount of raw data, or you need to generate a
[120](https://docs.rs#120)/// variably-sized collection type, or something of that sort. The
[121](https://docs.rs#121)/// [`Unstructured`] type helps you with these tasks.
[122](https://docs.rs#122)///
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// ```
[124](https://docs.rs#124)/// # #[cfg(feature = "derive")] mod foo {
[125](https://docs.rs#125)/// # pub struct MyCollection<T> { _t: std::marker::PhantomData<T> }
[126](https://docs.rs#126)/// # impl<T> MyCollection<T> {
[127](https://docs.rs#127)/// #     pub fn new() -> Self { MyCollection { _t: std::marker::PhantomData } }
[128](https://docs.rs#128)/// #     pub fn insert(&mut self, element: T) {}
[129](https://docs.rs#129)/// # }
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Result, Unstructured};
[131](https://docs.rs#131)///
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// impl<'a, T> Arbitrary<'a> for MyCollection<T>
[133](https://docs.rs#133)/// where
[134](https://docs.rs#134)///     T: Arbitrary<'a>,
[135](https://docs.rs#135)/// {
[136](https://docs.rs#136)///     fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
[137](https://docs.rs#137)///         // Get an iterator of arbitrary `T`s.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)///         let iter = u.arbitrary_iter::<T>()?;
[139](https://docs.rs#139)///
[140](https://docs.rs#140)///         // And then create a collection!
[141](https://docs.rs#141)///         let mut my_collection = MyCollection::new();
[142](https://docs.rs#142)///         for elem_result in iter {
[143](https://docs.rs#143)///             let elem = elem_result?;
[144](https://docs.rs#144)///             my_collection.insert(elem);
[145](https://docs.rs#145)///         }
[146](https://docs.rs#146)///
[147](https://docs.rs#147)///         Ok(my_collection)
[148](https://docs.rs#148)///     }
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// }
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// # }
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// ```
[152](https://docs.rs#152)///
[153](https://docs.rs#153)/// # A Note On Output Distributions
[154](https://docs.rs#154)///
[155](https://docs.rs#155)/// There is no requirement for a particular distribution of the values. For
[156](https://docs.rs#156)/// example, it is not required that every value appears with the same
[157](https://docs.rs#157)/// probability. That being said, the main use for `Arbitrary` is for fuzzing,
[158](https://docs.rs#158)/// so in many cases a uniform distribution will make the most sense in order to
[159](https://docs.rs#159)/// provide the best coverage of the domain. In other cases this is not
[160](https://docs.rs#160)/// desirable or even possible, for example when sampling from a uniform
[161](https://docs.rs#161)/// distribution is computationally expensive or in the case of collections that
[162](https://docs.rs#162)/// may grow indefinitely.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)pub trait Arbitrary<'a>: Sized {
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    /// Generate an arbitrary value of `Self` from the given unstructured data.
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    ///
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    /// Calling `Arbitrary::arbitrary` requires that you have some raw data,
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    /// perhaps given to you by a fuzzer like AFL or libFuzzer. You wrap this
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    /// raw data in an `Unstructured`, and then you can call `<MyType as
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    /// Arbitrary>::arbitrary` to construct an arbitrary instance of `MyType`
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// from that unstructured data.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    ///
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// Implementations may return an error if there is not enough data to
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    /// construct a full instance of `Self`, or they may fill out the rest of
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    /// `Self` with dummy values. Using dummy values when the underlying data is
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    /// exhausted can help avoid accidentally "defeating" some of the fuzzer's
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// mutations to the underlying byte stream that might otherwise lead to
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    /// interesting runtime behavior or new code coverage if only we had just a
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    /// few more bytes. However, it also requires that implementations for
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// recursive types (e.g. `struct Foo(Option<Box<Foo>>)`) avoid infinite
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// recursion when the underlying data is exhausted.
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    ///
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    /// ```
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// # #[cfg(feature = "derive")] fn foo() {
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    /// use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Unstructured};
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    ///
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    /// #[derive(Arbitrary)]
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    /// pub struct MyType {
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    ///     // ...
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    /// }
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    ///
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// // Get the raw data from the fuzzer or wherever else.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    /// # let get_raw_data_from_fuzzer = || &[];
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    /// let raw_data: &[u8] = get_raw_data_from_fuzzer();
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    ///
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    /// // Wrap that raw data in an `Unstructured`.
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    /// let mut unstructured = Unstructured::new(raw_data);
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    ///
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    /// // Generate an arbitrary instance of `MyType` and do stuff with it.
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// if let Ok(value) = MyType::arbitrary(&mut unstructured) {
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    /// #   let do_stuff = |_| {};
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    ///     do_stuff(value);
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    /// }
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    /// # }
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    /// ```
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    ///
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    /// See also the documentation for [`Unstructured`].
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self>;
[208](https://docs.rs#208)
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    /// Generate an arbitrary value of `Self` from the entirety of the given
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    /// unstructured data.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    ///
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    /// This is similar to Arbitrary::arbitrary, however it assumes that it is
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    /// the last consumer of the given data, and is thus able to consume it all
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    /// if it needs.  See also the documentation for
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    /// [`Unstructured`].
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    fn arbitrary_take_rest(mut u: Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        Self::arbitrary(&mut u)
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    }
[219](https://docs.rs#219)
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    /// Get a size hint for how many bytes out of an `Unstructured` this type
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    /// needs to construct itself.
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    ///
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    /// This is useful for determining how many elements we should insert when
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// creating an arbitrary collection.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    ///
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    /// The return value is similar to [`Iterator::size_hint`]: it returns a
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    /// tuple where the first element is a lower bound on the number of bytes
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// required, and the second element is an optional upper bound.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    ///
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    /// The default implementation return `(0, None)` which is correct for any
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    /// type, but not ultimately that useful. Using `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` will
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// create a better implementation. If you are writing an `Arbitrary`
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// implementation by hand, and your type can be part of a dynamically sized
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    /// collection (such as `Vec`), you are strongly encouraged to override this
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    /// default with a better implementation, and also override
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    /// [`try_size_hint`].
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    ///
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    /// ## How to implement this
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    ///
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    /// If the size hint calculation is a trivial constant and does not recurse
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// into any other `size_hint` call, you should implement it in `size_hint`:
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    ///
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    /// ```
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    /// use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, Result, Unstructured};
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    ///
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// struct SomeStruct(u8);
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    ///
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    /// impl<'a> Arbitrary<'a> for SomeStruct {
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    ///     fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    ///         let buf = &mut [0];
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    ///         u.fill_buffer(buf)?;
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    ///         Ok(SomeStruct(buf[0]))
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    ///     }
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    ///
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    ///     #[inline]
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    ///     fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    ///         let _ = depth;
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///         (1, Some(1))
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    ///     }
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    /// }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// ```
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    ///
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    /// Otherwise, it should instead be implemented in [`try_size_hint`],
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    /// and the `size_hint` implementation should forward to it:
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    ///
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    /// ```
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, MaxRecursionReached, Result, Unstructured};
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    ///
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// struct SomeStruct<A, B> {
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    ///     a: A,
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    ///     b: B,
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    /// }
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    ///
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// impl<'a, A: Arbitrary<'a>, B: Arbitrary<'a>> Arbitrary<'a> for SomeStruct<A, B> {
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    ///     fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    ///         // ...
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// #       todo!()
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    ///     }
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    ///
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    ///     fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    ///         // Return the value of try_size_hint
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    ///         //
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    ///         // If the recursion fails, return the default, always valid `(0, None)`
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    ///         Self::try_size_hint(depth).unwrap_or_default()
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    ///     }
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    ///
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    ///     fn try_size_hint(depth: usize) -> Result<(usize, Option<usize>), MaxRecursionReached> {
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    ///         // Protect against potential infinite recursion with
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    ///         // `try_recursion_guard`.
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    ///         size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth, |depth| {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    ///             // If we aren't too deep, then `recursion_guard` calls
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    ///             // this closure, which implements the natural size hint.
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    ///             // Don't forget to use the new `depth` in all nested
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    ///             // `try_size_hint` calls! We recommend shadowing the
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    ///             // parameter, like what is done here, so that you can't
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    ///             // accidentally use the wrong depth.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    ///             Ok(size_hint::and(
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    ///                 <A as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    ///                 <B as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    ///             ))
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    ///         })
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    ///     }
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    /// }
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    /// ```
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    ///
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    /// ## Invariant
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    ///
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    /// It must be possible to construct every possible output using only inputs
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// of lengths bounded by these parameters. This applies to both
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    /// [`Arbitrary::arbitrary`] and [`Arbitrary::arbitrary_take_rest`].
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    ///
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// This is trivially true for `(0, None)`. To restrict this further, it
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    /// must be proven that all inputs that are now excluded produced redundant
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    /// outputs which are still possible to produce using the reduced input
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// space.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    ///
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    /// [iterator-size-hint]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.size_hint
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    /// [`try_size_hint`]: Arbitrary::try_size_hint
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    #[inline]
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        let _ = depth;
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        (0, None)
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    }
[324](https://docs.rs#324)
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    /// Get a size hint for how many bytes out of an `Unstructured` this type
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    /// needs to construct itself.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    ///
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    /// Unlike [`size_hint`], this function keeps the information that the
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    /// recursion limit was reached. This is required to "short circuit" the
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    /// calculation and avoid exponential blowup with recursive structures.
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    ///
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    /// If you are implementing [`size_hint`] for a struct that could be
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    /// recursive, you should implement `try_size_hint` and call the
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    /// `try_size_hint` when recursing
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    ///
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    ///
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    /// The return value is similar to [`core::iter::Iterator::size_hint`]: it
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    /// returns a tuple where the first element is a lower bound on the number
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    /// of bytes required, and the second element is an optional upper bound.
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    ///
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    /// The default implementation returns the value of [`size_hint`] which is
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// correct for any type, but might lead to exponential blowup when dealing
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    /// with recursive types.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    ///
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    /// ## Invariant
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    ///
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    /// It must be possible to construct every possible output using only inputs
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    /// of lengths bounded by these parameters. This applies to both
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    /// [`Arbitrary::arbitrary`] and [`Arbitrary::arbitrary_take_rest`].
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    ///
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    /// This is trivially true for `(0, None)`. To restrict this further, it
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    /// must be proven that all inputs that are now excluded produced redundant
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    /// outputs which are still possible to produce using the reduced input
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    /// space.
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    ///
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    /// ## When to implement `try_size_hint`
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    ///
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    /// If you 100% know that the type you are implementing `Arbitrary` for is
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    /// not a recursive type, or your implementation is not transitively calling
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// any other `size_hint` methods, you may implement [`size_hint`], and the
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    /// default `try_size_hint` implementation will use it.
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    ///
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// Note that if you are implementing `Arbitrary` for a generic type, you
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// cannot guarantee the lack of type recursion!
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    ///
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    /// Otherwise, when there is possible type recursion, you should implement
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// `try_size_hint` instead.
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    ///
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// ## The `depth` parameter
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    ///
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    /// When implementing `try_size_hint`, you need to use
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    /// [`arbitrary::size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth)`][crate::size_hint::try_recursion_guard]
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    /// to prevent potential infinite recursion when calculating size hints for
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    /// potentially recursive types:
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    ///
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    /// ```
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    /// use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, MaxRecursionReached, Unstructured};
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    ///
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    /// // This can potentially be a recursive type if `L` or `R` contain
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// // something like `Box<Option<MyEither<L, R>>>`!
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    /// enum MyEither<L, R> {
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    ///     Left(L),
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    ///     Right(R),
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// }
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    ///
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    /// impl<'a, L, R> Arbitrary<'a> for MyEither<L, R>
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    /// where
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    ///     L: Arbitrary<'a>,
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    ///     R: Arbitrary<'a>,
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    /// {
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    ///     fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured) -> arbitrary::Result<Self> {
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    ///         // ...
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    /// #       unimplemented!()
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    ///     }
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    ///
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    ///     fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    ///         // Return the value of `try_size_hint`
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    ///         //
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    ///         // If the recursion fails, return the default `(0, None)` range,
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    ///         // which is always valid.
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    ///         Self::try_size_hint(depth).unwrap_or_default()
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    ///     }
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    ///
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    ///     fn try_size_hint(depth: usize) -> Result<(usize, Option<usize>), MaxRecursionReached> {
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    ///         // Protect against potential infinite recursion with
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    ///         // `try_recursion_guard`.
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    ///         size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth, |depth| {
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    ///             // If we aren't too deep, then `recursion_guard` calls
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    ///             // this closure, which implements the natural size hint.
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    ///             // Don't forget to use the new `depth` in all nested
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    ///             // `try_size_hint` calls! We recommend shadowing the
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    ///             // parameter, like what is done here, so that you can't
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    ///             // accidentally use the wrong depth.
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    ///             Ok(size_hint::or(
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    ///                 <L as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    ///                 <R as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    ///             ))
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    ///         })
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    ///     }
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    /// }
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    /// ```
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    #[inline]
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    fn try_size_hint(depth: usize) -> Result<(usize, Option<usize>), MaxRecursionReached> {
[424](https://docs.rs#424)        Ok(Self::size_hint(depth))
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    }
[426](https://docs.rs#426)}
[427](https://docs.rs#427)
[428](https://docs.rs#428)#[cfg(test)]
[429](https://docs.rs#429)mod test {
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    use super::*;
[431](https://docs.rs#431)
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    #[test]
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    fn exhausted_entropy() {
[434](https://docs.rs#434)        let mut u = Unstructured::new(&[]);
[435](https://docs.rs#435)        assert_eq!(u.arbitrary::<bool>().unwrap(), false);
[436](https://docs.rs#436)        assert_eq!(u.arbitrary::<u8>().unwrap(), 0);
[437](https://docs.rs#437)        assert_eq!(u.arbitrary::<usize>().unwrap(), 0);
[438](https://docs.rs#438)        assert_eq!(u.arbitrary::<f32>().unwrap(), 0.0);
[439](https://docs.rs#439)        assert_eq!(u.arbitrary::<f64>().unwrap(), 0.0);
[440](https://docs.rs#440)        assert_eq!(u.arbitrary::<Option<u32>>().unwrap(), None);
[441](https://docs.rs#441)        assert_eq!(u.int_in_range(4..=100).unwrap(), 4);
[442](https://docs.rs#442)        assert_eq!(u.choose_index(10).unwrap(), 0);
[443](https://docs.rs#443)        assert_eq!(u.ratio(5, 7).unwrap(), true);
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    }
[445](https://docs.rs#445)}
[446](https://docs.rs#446)

[561](https://docs.rs#561)    // Hidden trait that papers over the difference between `&mut Unstructured` and
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    // `Unstructured` arguments so that `with_recursive_count` can be used for both
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    // `arbitrary` and `arbitrary_take_rest`.

[579](https://docs.rs#579)
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    // Calls `f` with a recursive count guard.
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    #[inline]
[582](https://docs.rs#582)    pub fn with_recursive_count<U: IsEmpty, R>(
[583](https://docs.rs#583)        u: U,
[584](https://docs.rs#584)        recursive_count: &'static std::thread::LocalKey<std::cell::Cell<u32>>,
[585](https://docs.rs#585)        f: impl FnOnce(U) -> Result<R>,
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    ) -> Result<R> {
[587](https://docs.rs#587)        let guard_against_recursion = u.is_empty();
[588](https://docs.rs#588)        if guard_against_recursion {
[589](https://docs.rs#589)            recursive_count.with(|count| {
[590](https://docs.rs#590)                if count.get() > 0 {
[591](https://docs.rs#591)                    return Err(Error::NotEnoughData);
[592](https://docs.rs#592)                }
[593](https://docs.rs#593)                count.set(count.get() + 1);
[594](https://docs.rs#594)                Ok(())
[595](https://docs.rs#595)            })?;
[596](https://docs.rs#596)        }
[597](https://docs.rs#597)
[598](https://docs.rs#598)        let result = f(u);
[599](https://docs.rs#599)
[600](https://docs.rs#600)        if guard_against_recursion {
[601](https://docs.rs#601)            recursive_count.with(|count| {
[602](https://docs.rs#602)                count.set(count.get() - 1);
[603](https://docs.rs#603)            });
[604](https://docs.rs#604)        }
[605](https://docs.rs#605)
[606](https://docs.rs#606)        result
[607](https://docs.rs#607)    }

# Arbitrary in arbitrary - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arbitrary/1.4.2/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html

    // Required method

    fn [arbitrary_take_rest](https://docs.rs#method.arbitrary_take_rest)(u: [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self> { ... }
